tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the same Figure 9 (cfold time C++ 3.33, peak working set C++ 2.94, relative to Koka 1.00) is in the Perceus paper (MSR-TR-2020-42 v4, the extended version of the peer-reviewed PLDI 2021 paper, opened), with gcc 9.3.0 and AMD 3600XT stated. Not A: compile flags are not stated with the results (only derivable from CMake's Release default and the v2.0.3 Koka compiler source), and the run is first-party on code since revised.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Perceus TR Figure 9 (identical chart in the README, doc/bench-amd3600-nov-2020.png), normalized to Koka = 1.00: cfold execution time C++ 3.33 (Koka about 3.3x faster), peak working set C++ 2.94x. Koka 'no-opt' (reuse analysis and drop/reuse specialization off) is 1.54, so even without reuse Koka is about 2.2x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Other rows of the same figure: deriv C++ 1.33, rbtree C++ 0.92 and nqueens C++ 0.79 (C++ faster), rbtree-ck no C++ version.
corrections.baseline: C++ port in test/bench/cpp/cfold.cpp (gcc 9.3.0, CMake Release -O3, standard libc allocator): allocates every node with new and never frees anything, and its const_folding only folds the root node (no recursion into children), unlike the recursive Koka cfold.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Koka 2.0.3 -O2 (test/bench/koka/CMakeLists.txt), which the v2.0.3 compiler (src/Compiler/Options.hs) turns into gcc 9.3.0 '-O2 -flto -DNDEBUG' on the generated C, linked with Koka's bundled mimalloc (KK_MIMALLOC, MI_MAX_ALIGN_SIZE=8; the paper says 'a customized version of the mimalloc allocator'); C++: gcc 9.3.0, C++17, built through test/bench/CMakeLists.txt with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release and no extra flags in cpp/CMakeLists.txt, so CMake's default '-O3 -DNDEBUG', standard libc allocator. Flags are derived from the public build files, not printed with the results. Current Koka (v3.2.x) uses gcc -O2 -DNDEBUG -march=haswell instead.
corrections.hardware: 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 3600XT at 3.8 GHz, 64 GiB 3600 MHz memory, Ubuntu 20.04, November 2020; README says averaged over 10 runs, the Perceus tech report says median over 10 runs
corrections.caveats: The paper and README say the results are 'not a direct comparison of absolute performance between systems'. Not like-for-like: the C++ version never reclaims memory (glibc malloc, peak working set 2.94x Koka) while Koka frees and reuses nodes in place with mimalloc, and the C++ const_folding is shallow (does strictly less work than Koka's recursive cfold; the eval checksum is unchanged either way). An arena or pooled C++ version, or C++ linked against mimalloc, was not tried. Numbers are from Koka 2.0.3 and gcc 9.3.0 in November 2020; Koka is now v3.2.9 with different C flags. Koka ints are arbitrary-precision with a small-int fast path, C++ uses long. Mixed results across the suite: C++ wins rbtree (0.92) and nqueens (0.79).
corrections.why_faster: From the Perceus paper and build sources: Koka's generated C uses a customized mimalloc and garbage-free Perceus reference counting with reuse analysis (append_add/append_mul rebuild unique nodes in place), while the C++ baseline calls the standard libc operator new per node and never frees, so it runs with about 2.9x the working set. Koka 'no-opt' at 1.54 vs C++ 3.33 shows most of the gap is allocator and memory footprint rather than reuse or code generation; the win is the runtime's memory management, not the language's codegen.

notes: Numbers verified on the README chart and the Perceus TR figure; same chart, so cfold 3.33x time and 2.94x RSS are correct. Shortcomings to record: C++ baseline leaks every node and its const_folding is non-recursive (different algorithm, same_algorithm false), Koka links mimalloc versus glibc malloc on the C++ side (part of the win belongs to mimalloc, check against the listed mimalloc entry), authors disclaim it as an absolute speed comparison, 2020 Koka 2.0.3 numbers, C++ wins rbtree and nqueens. tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: benchLANG is a third-party suite with public code (languages/Nim/bench.nim, languages/C/bench.c, languages/C++/bench.cpp, run_benchmarks.sh, Nix flake), compilers (GCC 16.2.0, Nim 2.2.10), exact build flags for every language and the CPU (Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz) all stated; README table shows Nim 0.809 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s. A missing mechanism is not a tier criterion.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.10: nim c --hints:off --nimcache:nimcache -d:danger -d:lto --panics:on --passC:-march=native --passC:-ffp-contract=off --passL:-s; Nim's config/nim.cfg (v2.2.10) adds gcc.options.speed '-O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno' and -flto under -d:lto, so the generated C is built at -O3 -march=native -flto (backend gcc from the Nix dev shell, which uses gcc16Stdenv; the exact backend gcc version is not printed). Default Nim 2 memory management (ORC) and Nim's own allocator (no -d:useMalloc). C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags (GCC 16.2.0, nixpkgs-unstable).
corrections.caveats: One run per language on one machine (run_benchmarks.sh defaults to RUNS=1), so a 0.2 s gap is within plausible run-to-run noise; inputs are compile-time constants. Same algorithm and same work on both sides (C frees each tree inside the timed region, Nim's ORC destructors free at scope exit). The win is allocator behaviour: C and C++ pay glibc malloc/free (new/delete) per 24-byte node, while Nim uses its own runtime allocator; a pooled or arena C version, or C linked with a faster malloc, would likely erase the gap (my inference, not measured). Many other languages also beat C here (Java 0.347 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml and Dart 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s, Fortran 0.986 s). C is faster over the whole suite (9.762 s vs Nim 10.298 s); Nim loses strings (2.804 vs 2.132 s). 8-star suite.
corrections.why_faster: Inferred from the sources (the suite states no mechanism): Nim 'ref object' nodes are allocated by Nim's built-in runtime allocator and freed deterministically by ORC/ARC destructors, while the C and C++ versions call glibc malloc/free and operator new/delete per node; the gap is allocator throughput, not code generation (C, C++ and Nim tie on primes, Fibonacci and Mandelbrot).

notes: Numbers match the README table (Nim 0.809 s, C 1.010 s, C++ 1.147 s; 1.25x vs C and 1.42x vs C++ derived from page data). Shortcomings to record: single run, allocator-driven win (glibc malloc baseline), many languages including Java beat C on this workload, C faster overall, small 8-star suite. MIT, last commit 2026-09-03, active.
